title: Preparing for the introduction of HPV vaccines : policy and programme guidance for countries

sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: The front matter of WHO's 2006 guidance 'Preparing for the introduction of HPV vaccines: policy and programme guidance for countries', with copyright, disclaimers and a contents list. It notes that the content draws on a March 2006 technical consultation in Montreux on sexual and reproductive health programmes and HPV vaccines and lists the participating experts. The acknowledgements name the UNFPA and WHO departments involved and say the note aims to alert stakeholders in several health programmes to key issues.

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Explains that the guidance highlights how immunization, sexual and reproductive health and cancer control programmes can prepare for national HPV vaccine introduction under the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy.

sections.extract: cer. In particular, it highlights the contributions that national immunization programmes, sexual and reproductive health programmes, and cancer con- trol programmes can make in preparing for national introduction of the vaccines in the context of the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy.

sections.title: Cervical cancer and HPV infection

summary.text: Describes cervical cancer as the second most common cancer in women worldwide, with about 500 000 cases and 250 000 deaths a year, mostly in low-income countries, and nearly all linked to HPV infection, especially types 16 and 18. It explains that HPV infection usually clears but can persist and lead to precancerous lesions over decades, which screening can detect, and that visual inspection with acetic acid and cryotherapy offer a simpler approach for low-resource settings. It also notes the 2005 World Health Assembly resolution on cancer prevention and control and early vaccine trial results showing near-complete protection.

sections.extract: infection Cancer of the cervix is the second most common cancer in women worldwide, with about 500 000 new cases and 250 000 deaths each year. Almost 80% of cases occur in low-income countries, where cervical cancer is the most common cancer in women. Virtually all cervical cancer cases (99%) are linked to genital infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), which is the most common viral infection of the reproductive

sections.title: Vaccines against HPV V V

summary.text: Explains that HPV vaccines are made of non-infectious virus-like particles and that two prophylactic vaccines have shown excellent efficacy against precancerous lesions linked to the vaccine types, with the quadrivalent vaccine also preventing genital warts. It notes the vaccines are expected to prevent about 70% of cervical cancers in HPV-naive women and that questions on long-term efficacy, boosters and special populations are still being studied.

sections.extract: HPV vaccines contain the major capsid L1 proteins, which self-assemble into virus-like particles (VLP) resembling HPV. These particles do not contain viral genetic material and thus are unable to multiply, which means they are non-infectious. sections.title: Target populations for HPV immunization

summary.text: Argues that HPV vaccines should be given before sexual debut and notes they will likely be licensed for girls and women aged 9–26, with stronger immune responses in young adolescents and possible catch-up vaccination. It describes the expected availability of Cervarix and Gardasil and the uncertain benefit of vaccinating males, younger children, people with HIV and pregnant women. It links vaccine introduction to WHO's reproductive health strategy and its call to use existing services as entry points.

sections.extract: HPV immunization In deﬁ ning the target population for immunization, a key consideration is that HPV infection is sexually transmitted and is usually acquired within the ﬁ rst few years following sexual debut. Ideally, therefore, the vaccine should be administered before sexual debut, i.e. before any risk of exposure to HPV. sections.title: Innovative features of HPV vaccines

summary.text: Notes that HPV vaccines could strengthen links between health services and prevent a common cancer as well as genital dysplasia and warts on a large scale, and introduces their key features.

sections.extract: HPV vaccines HPV vaccines have the potential to strengthen interactions among different health services and to provide a new way of preventing a common cancer on a very large scale, as well as reducing the more widespread burden of genital dysplasia and warts. Some of the key features of the vaccines are dis- cussed below.

sections.title: A unique opportunity

summary.text: Explains that HPV vaccines need new delivery approaches because they target adolescents rather than infants, involve many stakeholders and bring immunization programmes into the sensitive area of sexual health. It describes the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy's aim to extend immunization to other age groups and the hard priority choices cancer programmes face. It sees the vaccines as a chance to promote delayed sexual debut and condom use, which will depend on strong partnerships between programmes.

sections.extract: Vaccines against HPV have several features that require special consideration. Their use requires new approaches to programme delivery; the target population is different from that usually addressed by national immunization programmes; multiple stakeholders need to be involved in advocacy and social communication; and the best combination of vaccination and screening for cervical cancer programmes remains unclear.

sections.title: An expensive product

summary.text: Notes that HPV vaccines are likely to cost much more than traditional EPI vaccines and that international financing, for example through GAVI, is being discussed. It warns that cost should not be the only criterion and that private-sector introduction among affluent groups could widen health inequities.

sections.extract: Although the price of HPV vaccines for developing countries is not yet known, it is likely to be sub- stantially higher than the traditional EPI vaccines, at least initially, even with differential pricing between developed- and developing-country markets. Discussions are under way to obtain access to international ﬁ nancing mechanisms (e.g. through the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immuniza- tion – GAVI), which

sections.title: Introduction challenges

summary.text: Stresses that HPV vaccine delivery must be affordable, feasible and culturally acceptable and that backlash against sexual and reproductive health programmes must be avoided. It calls for clear complementary messages on delaying sex, condom use, HIV prevention and screening, and hopes the vaccine will spur cervical screening where it is lacking.

sections.extract: The service delivery strategy and promotion of HPV vaccines will need to be based on country-spe- ciﬁ c considerations of what is affordable, feasible and culturally acceptable. Vaccinating young girls against cancer, and other genital diseases, caused by a sexually transmitted infection may be a sensi- tive issue in some countries and cultural settings. It will be essential to avoid a harmful backlash against

sections.title: Not business as usual

summary.text: Argues that programmes must find new ways of working together and with the private sector, and that international partnerships are needed to shorten delays in vaccine access for developing countries. It highlights the challenge of balanced communication about the vaccines' benefits and limits and of presenting them within a wider strategy to prevent cervical cancer deaths.

sections.extract: The unique features and characteristics of the HPV vaccines mean that all the concerned programmes in each country will be challenged to ﬁ nd new ways of working together. Moreover, as mentioned above, public programmes will need to act in concert with the private sector. At international level, partnerships need to be established now to try to reduce the usual lag time between formal registration and availability

sections.title: Advocacy, information and communication

summary.text: Sets out key messages for presenting HPV vaccines, such as HPV causing over 99% of cervical cancers, being very common and highly transmissible, and often having no symptoms. It notes the vaccines' high efficacy in HPV-naive young women and stresses explaining clearly what they can and cannot do, alongside lifestyle information for young people.

sections.extract: communication Developing advocacy, information and commu- nication programmes related to HPV vaccination, for multiple stakeholders and audiences, presents speciﬁ c challenges and opportunities. sections.title: Action points

summary.text: Lists action points on advocacy, information and communication, such as gathering country data on cancer burden and HPV strains, tailoring communication strategies to stakeholders, decision-makers and communities, and basing health promotion on local needs. It also covers developing materials and training for health workers and addressing financing questions such as insurance coverage. It urges using HPV vaccination to strengthen existing programmes for adolescents, such as school-based education on sexual health, nutrition, tobacco and HIV.

sections.title: Reaching target populations
sections.extract: populations The vaccine licences will probably establish an age range of 9–26 years for the target population. This age range will need to be subdivided into two cat- egories: the primary group and the catch-up group. Primary target population This will most likely be girls aged 9–13 years, the intention being to reach them prior to sexual debut. Each country will need to identify the most con- venient and effective

sections.title: Partnerships between programmes

summary.text: Recommends building HPV vaccine delivery on existing structures such as the cold chain, with the immunization programme likely leading in partnership with sexual and reproductive health, adolescent health, cancer control and HIV programmes. It also calls for links with education services, civil society and the private sector.

sections.extract: programmes Programme approaches will need to be planned and organized, making the most cost-efﬁ cient use of existing or, where necessary, strengthened services. HPV vaccine delivery should be built on structures already in place at the national level, for example, the vaccine cold chain infrastruc- ture. This will maximize cost-efﬁ ciency and avoid wastage and duplication, which countries can ill afford. While it

sections.title: Monitoring and evaluation

summary.text: Advises planning early for monitoring and evaluation, using routine immunization surveillance for process indicators and tracking earlier outcomes such as genital warts and precancerous lesions. It also calls for adverse event monitoring that captures HIV status and pregnancy, use of cancer registries or proxies, and private-sector cooperation on reporting.

sections.extract: Although the construction of an effective monitoring and evaluation system is a “downstream” activity, it is important during the preparatory stage to con- sider how to assess process and impact. Process indicators will have to be measured through routine national immunization programme surveillance. sections.title: Action points

summary.text: Lists action points for national programmes on service delivery, such as linking stakeholders, defining the primary target group, addressing sociocultural barriers, checking school attendance and updating cervical cancer strategies. It also calls for comprehensive cervical cancer prevention including screening, treatment, vaccination and monitoring of effectiveness.

sections.extract: National programmes will need to undertake the following actions: • Develop links between the many different imple- menting stakeholders. • Deﬁ ne the primary target population, taking into account the most convenient access points, and the earliest age of sexual debut. • Address sociocultural barriers to vaccination of young adolescents. • Determine school attendance rates for the 9–13-year age group. • Update

sections.title: Stewardship and ﬁ nancing

summary.text: Stresses that strengthening health systems and financing HPV vaccine purchase must be high priorities, with some decisions taken at global or higher government levels. It discusses the need for epidemiological data, demand forecasting and lessons from hepatitis B vaccine introduction, and the importance of international funding through GAVI, UNICEF and the PAHO Revolving Fund to expand supply and secure lower prices. It also covers government oversight of private-sector introduction, such as reporting of adverse events and post-marketing surveillance.

sections.extract: health system and purchasing HPV vaccines, both internationally and within national health budgets, must be a high priority. Financing for the introduc- tion of HPV vaccine will need to be approached as part of an overall strategy involving a number of partners, both globally and within individual countries, and be part of a general scaling-up of resources to strengthen health systems. sections.title: Action points

summary.text: Lists stewardship and financing actions, including setting up a national HPV vaccine working group, developing demand and financing models and a business case for public and private funding. It stresses integrated delivery, partnerships, closing knowledge gaps and developing detailed delivery guidelines.

sections.extract: In the area of stewardship and ﬁ nancing, the fol- lowing actions will need to be undertaken. • A broad range of stakeholders should be involved in developing a strategy for a com- prehensive and workable introduction of HPV vaccines. A national HPV vaccine working group should be established in each country to set up coordination mechanisms between health programmes, civil society and private sector. This could be

sections.title: Epilogue

summary.text: Concludes that the HPV vaccine is one element of comprehensive cervical cancer control and warns that, without attention to poorer women, it could widen health inequities. A note added in proof reports the US FDA's June 2006 approval of the quadrivalent vaccine Gardasil for girls and women aged 9–26 and lists the conditions it is intended to prevent.

sections.extract: Ultimately, the decision on whether and when to introduce an HPV vaccine will depend on national policy in each country. An overarching consid- eration is the importance of positioning the HPV vaccine within a comprehensive, integrated service delivery structure.
